## Summary

A state that lived on oil spent as if prices would stay high. When oil fell in 2014–15, it covered the gap with the central bank, while price and exchange controls had been emptying the shops since
2003. Hyperinflation began in **November 2016** and only ended technically in **early 2022**. The
highest monthly figure found so far is **192 % in January 2019 (National Assembly estimate)**.
Inflation figures for 2018 range from 130,060 % to 1,698,488 % depending on the source. The
bolívar lost 14 zeros in three redenominations (2008, 2018, 2021), and the economy turned to the
dollar.

## Causes

- **Dependence on oil.** Oil was almost all of Venezuela's exports. The 2014 price collapse cut
  both its dollar income and its tax revenue.
- **Price controls (since 2003) and exchange controls.** Shortages, smuggling, and a black-market
  dollar whose rate became the real price of everything.
- **The central bank financed the state.** The money supply grew 64 % in 2014, three times faster
  than in any other economy (Wikipedia).

## Timeline

- **2003** — exchange and price controls are introduced.
- **2008** — the bolívar fuerte (1,000 : 1).
- **2014–2015** — oil prices collapse.
- **Nov 2016** — hyperinflation begins.
- **2018** — annual inflation estimated between 130,060 % and 1,698,488 %, depending on the source.
- **20 Aug 2018** — the bolívar soberano (100,000 : 1).
- **Jan 2019** — 192 % in the month (National Assembly).
- **2019** — de facto dollarisation; controls are loosened.
- **Oct 2021** — the bolívar digital (1,000,000 : 1).
- **Q1 2022** — 12 months below 50 % a month: the hyperinflation is technically over.

## The end

There was no single reform. The end came from **de facto dollarisation**: prices, wages and savings moved to the dollar, and the state loosened controls and slowed the printing press.

## Lessons

- Official statistics stop being credible. Each figure has a source that has to be named.
